newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says won't budge on cautious China policy.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says won't budge on cautious China policy.

text.p: Taiwan's top economic policy maker said on Wednesday that Taipei had no immediate intention of easing its tough economic policy towards China and urged local firms to put the national interest above their own.

Chiang Pin-kung, chairman of the cabinet's Council for Economic Planning and Development, said Taiwan could not change its cautious mainland policy until Beijing demonstrated good faith in promoting genuine relations across the Taiwan strait.
"Taiwan's economic policy towards China cannot follow the pattern of free economy," Chiang told Reuters in an interview.
"Politically we are in a confrontation. Our relations are hostile," he said.
Taipei worries that its prosperous economy could become too dependent on China, leaving it politically vulnerable.
Beijing has regarded Nationalist-ruled Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949 and pledges to retake the island eventually, by force if necessary.
Taiwan forbids direct China investments, obliging firms to route even small investments through Hong Kong or other third territories after obtaining permits from the Economic Ministry.

Policies barring major infrastructure investments in China have come under fire in recent days due to a bid by the island's top industrial enterprise, Formosa Plastics group, to build a US$3 billion power station in Fujian province.

Formosa triggered a weekend of uncertainty by saying it was going ahead with the project in defiance of Taipei's wishes, but apparently backed down on Monday, pledging to respect the government's policy and abandon the giant investment.
Chiang urged Taiwanese businesses always to put the nation's interests above their own profits, saying the Formosa project would benefit Taiwan's rival but not Taiwan itself.
"It would not in any way benefit Taiwan's economy. It offers money to assist the other and the risk is great," Chiang said.

"They (Taiwan investors) should bear in mind that national security is the top priority," he added. "I don't see any reason for the government to let Taiwan companies invest in power stations or any large-scale public investments on the mainland."

Chiang, who is overseeing Taiwan's economic liberalisation, rejected criticism that Taipei had failed to enact clear guidelines for China investments, a shortcoming exposed by Formosa Plastics' decision to drop a power plant project.
But he agreed there was room for improvement.
"The government's economic policy toward the Chinese mainland is not ambiguous. As a citizen, you do what the law says you can do," Chiang said.
"But we may need to clarify the criteria so that businesses know what kind of project will be approved, what kind of project will be rejected," he said.
Some 30,000 Taiwan businesses have poured some US$30 billion into China since an unofficial thaw in ties began in the 1980s.
Asked under what circumstances the government would consider easing its mainland policy, Chiang said the resumption of bilateral negotiations would be a good start.
China angrily suspended semi-official talks between Taipei and Beijing in mid-1995 after Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui made a private but high-profile visit to the United States.
